subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
passage: "You look so sure of yourself when you read people, Pema," Ira said, pouring tea for her niece. "Let me tell you about the time I was wrong. I was twenty, standing at a bus stop in the early morning. A young man beside me had his shoulders pulled up near his ears, and he kept glancing round. I thought, he's frightened, someone must be after him. I even took a step toward the shopkeeper for help." She laughed. "Then I asked, 'Are you all right?' He said, 'It's freezing, and I forgot my jacket.' I wanted to vanish." Pema grinned. "So?" "So now I read the weather and the situation before I read the person. And if I'm unsure, I ask."

qa.q: Where was Ira standing when she saw the young man?
qa.a: She was standing at a bus stop in the early morning.

qa.q: What did Ira think when she saw his shoulders pulled up?
qa.a: She thought he was frightened and that someone might be after him, though he was only cold.

qa.q: What does Ira do now when she sees someone with raised shoulders?
qa.a: She considers the weather and the situation first, and asks if she is unsure.

qa.q: How might the young man have felt when Ira asked if he was all right?
qa.a: He was probably a little surprised and perhaps touched at her concern, even though the truth was only the cold.

grounding: A young adult sees raised shoulders and guesses fear, though it was cold, so context and asking come first.

passage: The power had been out in the hostel since afternoon, and a cold wind rattled the shutters. In the corridor Chaitanya spotted Lalit with his shoulders hunched up around his ears, staring at the floor, his phone dead in his hand. Chaitanya's mind jumped: exam results were due today, so Lalit must be afraid. He almost started a pep talk about not worrying. Then he noticed his own arms crossed against the chill, and Lalit's thin shirt. It was dark and freezing. He took a step closer and said, "Hey, you all right? Or is it just cold?" Lalit gave a short laugh. "Just cold. I left my sweater at the canteen." Chaitanya lent him his blanket.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt if Chaitanya had given a pep talk?

passage:
At the bus stop outside their college in Delhi, the December fog was so thick Dhruv could barely see the road. Bidisha stood a little apart from the others, shoulders raised almost to her ears, arms wrapped around herself.
Dhruv wondered. Was she scared? A man at the other end of the shelter had been looking around a lot. Or was she just freezing? She'd come from Kolkata only a month ago.
He didn't want to make it awkward. He walked over. "Hey, you okay? You look tense."
Bidisha laughed through chattering teeth. "Tense? I'm frozen! Nobody told me Delhi winter is like this. My jacket is useless."
Dhruv relaxed. "Ah. Cold, not scared."
"Very cold. A tiny bit scared of the fog. Mostly cold."
He handed her his spare muffler. "Keep it till you buy a real jacket."
Her shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: Where had Bidisha come from a month ago?
qa.a: From Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Bidisha actually feeling at the bus stop?
qa.a: Bidisha was mostly very cold, with only a little nervousness about the fog.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do before assuming?
qa.a: He looked at the context, then walked over and asked gently if she was okay, instead of guessing fear.

qa.q: How did Dhruv first read Bidisha's raised shoulders?
qa.a: He wondered if she was scared, possibly of the man in the shelter, before learning she was cold.

grounding: The scene shows raised shoulders that might signal fear being mostly about cold, with context and asking coming first.

passage:
"Urmila, you've been sitting like that for twenty minutes."
Urmila looked up from her notes in the hostel common room. Her shoulders were hunched up near her ears.
"Like what?"
"Like a turtle. Are you cold? The fan's on full."
"No. The fan's fine."
Maria sat down next to her. "Then what is it?"
Urmila's shoulders stayed up. "Viva tomorrow. The external examiner is the one who failed two students last year. I keep imagining him asking something I don't know."
"So scared, not cold."
"Very scared."
Maria nodded. "Want me to switch the fan off anyway?"
"No." Urmila almost smiled. "Can you just ask me the hardest questions? So I've heard them before he asks."
"Deal. First question. Why did you choose this topic?"
Urmila took a breath. As she started answering, her shoulders slowly came down.

qa.q: How many students had the external examiner failed last year?
qa.a: Two students.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling behind her raised shoulders?
qa.a: Urmila was scared and anxious about her viva with a strict external examiner.

qa.q: How did Maria find out what the raised shoulders meant?
qa.a: She considered the context, the fan, and then asked directly instead of assuming cold or fear.

qa.q: What did practising the hardest questions do for Urmila?
qa.a: It gave her a sense of control, and as she answered, her shoulders relaxed.

grounding: The dialogue shows raised shoulders that could be cold or fear, and context and asking revealing anxiety.

subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
passage:
On the night bus from Pune to Goa last winter, I noticed Sudha, a girl from my college, sitting two rows ahead with her shoulders pulled up tight, arms crossed. The AC was blasting.
I assumed she was cold, like me. At the next stop I went up and offered my jacket.
She shook her head quickly and whispered, "It's not the cold. That man behind me keeps leaning forward. He's touched my seat twice."
I felt awful. I'd almost walked away with my jacket and my wrong guess.
I said, "Want to swap seats with me?" She nodded. I sat in her seat, and she took mine next to an older woman.
Then I told the conductor. He moved the man to the back and checked on Sudha till Goa.
Now when I see raised shoulders, I don't jump to cold or to fear. I look around, and I ask.
- Irfan

qa.q: Where was the night bus going?
qa.a: From Pune to Goa.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling behind her raised shoulders?
qa.a: Sudha felt frightened and uncomfortable because the man behind her kept leaning forward and touching her seat.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's steps helped Sudha?
qa.a: Asking instead of only assuming cold, swapping seats with her, and telling the conductor, who moved the man and checked on her.

qa.q: How did Irfan first read Sudha's raised shoulders?
qa.a: Irfan assumed she was simply cold from the AC, like Irfan.

grounding: The account shows raised shoulders read as cold when they signalled fear, and context and asking coming first.

subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
passage:
Volunteer notes, winter camp at the station night shelter, 12 January.
A young man, Pradeep, came in late and stood by the door with his shoulders pulled up to his ears and his arms pressed to his sides. Two volunteers whispered that he looked frightened, maybe in some trouble, and suggested calling the shelter guard. Kiran, one of our second-year students, asked them to wait. She walked over slowly and said, "Long day? Are you cold, or is something worrying you?" Pradeep laughed through chattering teeth: his bus had broken down and he had walked an hour in the fog without a jacket. Kiran brought tea and a blanket and sat with him a while. Ten minutes later his shoulders had dropped and he was chatting about cricket. I have added "look at the context and ask before assuming" to tomorrow's briefing, and asked Kiran to tell the group what happened.

qa.q: Why had Pradeep walked an hour in the fog?
qa.a: His bus had broken down.

qa.q: What was Pradeep most likely feeling as he stood by the door?
qa.a: He was most likely cold and tired after a long walk in the fog; fear was a possible reading, but his chattering teeth and missing jacket pointed to cold.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do after the evening?
qa.a: The note-writer added "look at the context and ask before assuming" to the next day's briefing and asked Kiran to share what happened with the group.

qa.q: What would have changed if the volunteers had called the guard straight away?
qa.a: Pradeep, who was only cold and worn out, might have felt treated like a threat and could have left the shelter on a freezing night.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult seeing raised shoulders, holding back the guess of fear, and using context and a question to find the person was simply cold.
